transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-30
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Lighthouse Head Data), Omar Hatt (CTO), Ellen Brooks (ML Eng), Samir Patel (Infra)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Redwood and Lighthouse kicked off a technical POC to validate OpenAI-compatible SDK integration, structured output templates, and function/tool-calling for Lighthouse's field-report summarization workloads. Discussed workload sizing (concurrent sessions, average token lengths), benchmark plan, success criteria (latency p95 < 350ms, cost per 1k tokens target, quality pass rate on eval set), and timeline for a 3-week sprint + 2-week benchmark run. Security (VPC/private deployment, KMS, audit logs) and network pairing were raised as gating items. Next steps include sharing benchmark harness, sample prompts, and scheduling a deep dive on private deployment networking.

Topics covered:
- POC goals & success criteria
- Workload characteristics and sizing
- Benchmark harness and metrics (latency, throughput, quality)
- SDK & OpenAI-compatible endpoint integration
- Function/tool calling and structured JSON output
- Private/VPC deployment, KMS, SOC2 and audit logs
- Timeline and sprint cadence

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Thanks everybody for taking the time, we'll keep this tight. Quick intros then jump to the POC goals.
[00:23] Priya (Lighthouse): Hi, I'm Priya. We're running this around field ops: lots of noisy inputs, transcripts from on-site voice->text, then we need structured incident summaries to feed downstream billing and analytics. Latency matters but quality is top.
[00:41] Omar (Lighthouse): Hi all, CTO here. We're also concerned about cost at scale, and whether we should go hosted first or straight to a private deployment.
[00:56] Maya (Redwood): Great. High level: we typically run a 3-week integration sprint to wire up SDKs and benchmarks, then a 2-week benchmark run at scale. The POC aims to validate OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function-calling reliability, structured output templates, and performance metrics.
[01:12] Diego (Redwood): From the SE side, we'll want sample prompts, typical token lengths, concurrency numbers, and an eval set. We'll provide a benchmark harness that hits the OpenAI-compatible API and measures latency, tokens/sec, memory usage, and error modes.
[01:31] Ellen (Lighthouse): On token lengths: average prompt+response is roughly 700 tokens, peak 2k for long incident write-ups. Concurrency: typically 50 steady concurrent requests, bursts to 300 during shift change.
[01:51] Priya: Yeah and we have a tail of long inferences cause of attachments and notes. We need structured JSON output with explicit fields: incident_type, severity, clean_summary, actions, participants.
[02:10] Maya: Perfect, that maps well. Success criteria we propose: p95 latency < 350ms for 700 token median, successful structured output parse rate > 95% on the canonical 1000-eval prompts, throughput target to sustain 300 concurrent at 1.2 requests/sec each without SLA breach, and cost target TBD by you.
[02:31] Omar: p95 350ms might be aggressive if we go hosted; is that for dedicated infra?
[02:40] Diego: Right, the SLO depends on deployment mode. On Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pool) or private we can get closer to that. Hosted adds multi-tenant variance. We should define two bands: hosted baseline and dedicated/private target.
[03:02] Samir (Lighthouse): For us, network egress and VPC peering constraints matter. If we're doing private deploy we need KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs pushed to our SIEM.
[03:18] Maya: Noted. We have a Private option with a customer-controlled control plane and KMS integrations (we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and HSM vendors via partners). We'll include a compliance pack (SOC2 artefacts, SSO/SAML notes).
[03:34] Priya: Can you send the security docs? Our compliance team will need SOC2 report and the data retention/audit log details.
[03:42] Maya: Yes, we'll attach the security whitepaper and a sample network diagram.
[03:46] Diego: For the benchmark harness, we usually ship a small container that replays prompt sets at configurable concurrency and collects per-call metrics including token breakdown, kv-cache hit ratio, GPU utilization (if dedicated), and latency percentiles. We'll also include a sample OpenAPI/SDK snippet in Python and Node.
[04:11] Priya: Do you support function-calling for tool invocation? We have a step where an external mapping service needs structured coords.
[04:19] Diego: Yes, Redwood supports function/tool calling and structured outputs. A couple of caveats from field experience: when using function-calling at high concurrency, ensure your tool/backend scales—Redwood can batch function calls or fall back to a safe mode. We'll demo the function call error modes.
[04:40] Ellen: Do you provide schema validation or structured output enforcement? We can't afford malformed JSON blobs in production.
[04:47] Diego: We have a validation layer in the runtime that can do post-generation schema checks, plus we recommend a two-pass pattern: generation then verify/repair prompt. We'll include a small router example that enforces JSON schema and returns repair prompts.
[05:03] Omar: About SDKs — we have a lot of existing code expecting OpenAI-compatible endpoints. How much effort to swap endpoints?
[05:12] Maya: Minimal. Our OpenAI-compatible endpoint mirrors request/response shapes. We provide client SDKs that are drop-in with a single config switch. We'll also share migration notes for streaming and function-calling differences.
[05:26] Priya: Any known incompatibilities?
[05:29] Diego: Occasionally model naming and streaming chunk formats vary; also the behavior around partial tokens during reconnects can differ. We'll include a compatibility checklist.
[05:44] Priya: Benchmarks—what metrics will you collect exactly?
[05:48] Diego: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens estimate, error rates, retry behavior, cold-start times for KV cache, and function-call success ratio. We'll also capture quality metrics using your eval set — fraction of outputs that pass schema and match ground-truth tags.
[06:12] Priya: For quality thresholds, we want >=95% schema pass, and human-validated relevance > 90% on a 200-sample check.
[06:22] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll use bot-holdout evaluation and also recommend a blinded human eval for the 200-sample.
[06:30] Omar: Timeline — you said 3-week sprint then 2-week benchmark run. Can we compress to 2+2? Q4 schedule is tight.
[06:39] Maya: We could compress if Lighthouse provides prompts and infrastructure access immediately. The risk is less time for infra/network validation. Proposed: Week 1 integration (SDK, endpoints, function-calling), Week 2 instrumentation + small-scale bench, Week 3 full run — compressing loses week 3.
[06:58] Samir: Network approvals usually take a week in our org. We'd prefer the normal 3-week cadence.
[07:05] Priya: We'll aim for the 3-week plan.
[07:08] Diego: Regarding workload sizing: please confirm average/peak tokens and concurrency in the doc you share. We'll size GPU needs and whether 2xA100-equivalent or 4xA100-equivalent pools are needed for the target throughput.
[07:23] Ellen: Also note the attachment parsing stage — we have OCR -> tokenization that sometimes adds 30% tokens.
[07:32] Diego: Good to know — that'll affect caching and batch sizes.
[07:38] Priya: Any suggestions for prompt engineering to reduce cost but preserve quality?
[07:42] Maya: We recommend structured prompts with explicit JSON scaffolding, use of system messages to limit verbosity, and prefix caching for repeated metadata. Also dynamic batching settings to balance latency/cost. We'll provide example prompts with several compression patterns.
[07:58] Omar: On private deployment, how do rollback and model pinning work during the POC? If we test a quantized variant and see quality drop, can we switch back?
[08:07] Diego: Yes — model versioning and canary rollouts are supported. The runtime supports fallback to a safe model variant automatically based on policy. We'll demo canary and A/B routing.
[08:21] Priya: For auditing, we need immutable logs and ability to replay requests for a month. Is that supported?
[08:28] Maya: We can provide audit logs and retention options as an add-on. For private customers we can ship logs to your S3 or GCS bucket and provide replay tooling. We'll include retention options in the compliance doc.
[08:44] Priya: Pricing — rough estimates for Dedicated for our expected baseline?
[08:49] Maya: We'll send a estimates sheet after we size the workload. For the POC we can do a temporary promo dedicated pool to run the benchmarks affordably.
[08:59] Samir: If we do private, any HSM integration lead time we should know?
[09:04] Diego: HSM integrations typically take 2-4 weeks to validate depending on vendor. If you need HSM in POC, we should start that parallel.
[09:12] Priya: Ok, we'll flag whether HSM is required in the doc.
[09:16] Maya: Next steps recap: Redwood to send benchmark harness, security pack, network diagram, SDK snippets, and a suggested sprint plan. Lighthouse to provide eval prompts, token/concurrency numbers, and network contacts for Samir.
[09:30] Ellen: Quick question — do you support partial responses streaming and resume? Our UI streams partial summaries.
[09:35] Diego: Yes, streaming is supported but behavior can vary with reconnects; we'll include best practices.
[09:41] Priya: Are there any licensing or data residency gotchas? We're UK and US operations.
[09:47] Maya: We have region-aware deployments and can pin data to regions for Private and Dedicated. Hosted may have cross-region fallback — we'll document data residency knobs.
[09:58] Omar: Anything else from Redwood?
[10:01] Maya: Nothing major. We'll follow-up in email with the harness and dates.
[10:05] Priya: We'll circulate our success criteria internally and reply with the canonical prompts.
[10:10] [cross talk / brief chatter about calendar invites]
[10:25] Diego: One more technical note — KV cache effectiveness: for repeated metadata you'll see big savings. We'll show cache hit ratio in the bench.
[10:37] Samir: For network, we'd like a diagram of peering and required ports so our security team can pre-approve.
[10:43] Maya: We'll attach a sample peering diagram.
[10:47] Omar: Great. End-of-call recap and action items?
[10:52] Maya: Recap: benchmark harness (Maya), initial throughput run (Diego), prompt set (Priya), network diagram + KMS info (Samir). We'll plan the kickoff sprint to begin after we get Samir's network details.
[11:07] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[11:10] Ellen: Thanks.
[11:12] Maya: Thanks all, I'll send the follow-up.

(Transcription notes: occasional mis-hearings, product names may be slightly off — e.g., 'Redwood Privat' or 'red wood' — and timestamps approximate. There was minor crosstalk when scheduling.)
